headline: The global bond selloff deepened as the US 10 year Treasury yield touched 5.344 percent, its highest since 2002, and the UK 30 year gilt broke 6 percent for the first time since 1998, knocking European equities 1 to 2 percent lower and UK bank stocks to their worst day since May, while US indices still edged up and Accenture posted its best day on record at 15.78 percent.

summary.us: The S&P 500 added 0.19 percent to 7,666.45 and the Nasdaq Composite 0.04 percent to 26,871.60 after recovering from a sharp intraday drop, as the 10 year Treasury yield pulled back from an intraday 5.344 percent, its highest since 2002, to close at 5.237 percent. Accenture drove the session, rising 15.78 percent after fourth quarter earnings per share of 3.29 dollars on 18.68 billion dollars of revenue beat LSEG consensus of 3.18 dollars and 18.03 billion, with new bookings of 22.2 billion dollars at a 1.2 book to bill; Disney fell 3.40 percent on a Goldman Sachs target cut and fresh job cuts.
summary.india: The Nifty 50 fell 0.88 percent to 22,421.95 and the Sensex 0.79 percent to 71,909.71, completing an eighth consecutive weekly loss, the longest such streak in 25 years, with foreign investors selling 9,484.20 crore rupees in cash against 10,041.80 crore of domestic buying and India VIX up 7.19 percent to 14.46. Nifty Auto was the worst sector at 3.46 percent lower after September sales missed, taking Bajaj Auto down 7.62 percent on a 9 percent domestic decline, while Nifty IT was the sole gainer at 2.17 percent as investors positioned into the Accenture result; markets are shut on 2 October for Gandhi Jayanti and reopen on 5 October as the RBI meets.
summary.global: The Nikkei 225 rose 3.3 percent on 1 October to 68,956.72 led by chip names after Micron guided first quarter revenue above estimates, with Advantest up more than 8 percent, while Hong Kong and mainland China were shut for National Day. Europe fell across the board as the UK 30 year gilt yield hit 6.029 percent, its highest since January 1998, and oil driven inflation fears built, taking the FTSE 100 down 1.68 percent, the CAC 40 down 1.62 percent and the DAX down 1.03 percent; the dollar index rose 0.66 percent to 102.115, a three month high, pushing EUR/USD to a 52 week low of 1.1237.

weekly.narrative: The bond market set the terms all week: the US 10 year Treasury yield reached 5.2251 percent on 24 September, its highest since June 2007, and the 30 year touched 5.47 percent, a 22 year high, on strong manufacturing surveys, hawkish Fed commentary and a poorly bid five year auction, which pushed the dollar index to a two month high. Equities absorbed it anyway, because a reported phased US and Iran arrangement to reopen the Strait of Hormuz took WTI down 7.84 percent on the week and because Meta's Muse AI agent kept re-rating the largest index weights, lifting Meta 12.9 percent over five sessions while knocking bank stocks on 23 September as investors weighed whether agents could shop deposit rates on a customer's behalf. India went the other way, undone by a domestic regulator rather than by yields, after the IRDAI consultation paper on insurance distribution economics proposed commission caps and a five year glide path on expenses of management, taking PB Fintech down 33.1 percent on the week and dragging Nifty 50 to a 0.88 percent weekly loss even after Friday's rebound. Precious metals broke their run, with gold off 2.36 percent and silver off 2.77 percent on the week as real yields and the dollar bit, though both recovered on Friday, and copper held a 2.48 percent weekly gain near its 22 September record; crypto diverged from that risk-off tone, with bitcoin adding 3.38 percent and capital rotating into compute and DeFi tokens even after the Bitget hack. Next week the macro calendar is a labour market week rather than an inflation one, with JOLTS on 30 September, ADP and ISM manufacturing on 1 October and jobless claims and factory orders on 2 October, before the RBI Monetary Policy Committee meets 5 to 7 October with the repo rate at 5.25 percent after four pauses.
